summary: A retrospective on how blockchain startups moved beyond cryptocurrency into supply chains, real estate, fashion, healthcare, IoT, AI and charitable giving. It traces milestones from Bitcoin and early firms like BitPay and Coinbase through the 2017 ICO frenzy to recent applications, with quotes from startup executives. It closes with the role of regulation, citing the Digital Ledger Technology Act of 2024.
one_line: Overview of blockchain startups' evolution from crypto payments to supply chain, real estate, healthcare, IoT, AI and social good, shaped by regulation.
key_facts: BitPay was founded in May 2011 and Coinbase in June 2012, early startups that simplified the use of cryptocurrencies.
Ethereum launched in July 2015 with smart contract functionality, marking blockchain's move toward broader application.
In September 2018, Hyperledger Grid was formed as a collaborative effort to streamline supply chains.
Melanie Johnson, CEO of SupplySight, said on October 12, 2019 that supply chain management was an ideal contender for blockchain integration due to its need for transparency and traceability.
In March 2020, Propy Inc. facilitated the first-ever entirely blockchain-based real estate transaction.
In July 2021, TraceFash, a blockchain startup, transformed how authenticity and ethical sourcing were verified in the fashion industry.
In 2022, MedChain deployed decentralized patient records and prescription tracking systems in healthcare.
Dr. Samantha Keen, MedChain's CTO, said on September 5, 2022 that blockchain's immutable nature could be the antidote to medical record manipulation and breaches.
SmartMesh, founded in February 2023, combines blockchain with the Internet of Things to create decentralized networks for smart cities.
DeepChain uses blockchain to enhance data integrity for AI model training; founder Alex Wright was quoted on June 8, 2023.
SocialCoin, launched on November 3, 2023, uses blockchain to ensure charitable donations reach intended recipients without misappropriation or unnecessary intermediaries.
The Digital Ledger Technology Act of 2024 set new governance benchmarks, helping startups navigate legal waters with confidence.
